Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. Lastly, we outline potential extensions to our work, including the handling of numerical data and generalized functional relationships. Overall, this research offers a starting point for addressing a broad spectrum of data handling problems that arise when dealing with inconsistencies in data tables. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The project code has been made available at https://github.com/yangwei-1998/SixDOPoseEstimation.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. Our comprehensive, high-speed capture of these processes also reveals the previously unobserved, partial-seal regime. Overall, our analysis offers a more precise understanding of the water-entry interactions in the surface-seal regime, previously not extensively explored. The accurate prediction of pinch-off times is crucial in water-entry interactions, especially in cases where underwater explosions occur. The analysis provided in this paper offers valuable insights for developing more efficient rules that can be applied across a broader range of speeds. The study utilizes high-speed capture techniques, involving a 50-kilogram sphere with a 0.102-meter diameter, and modifies the existing rules to better suit the surface-seal regime, where the sphere interacts with a 1-meter deep water surface at mid-range speeds. The findings presented in this paper may be applied to larger-sized spheres, due to the speed-independent scale effect observed in this specific speed range. The research reveals the challenges and limitations of modeling the surface-seal regime using existing models, and highlights the need for new models that can effectively capture the dynamics of the rippling-cavity-surface stage. The most compelling feature of this research is the visual capture of the previously unobserved partial-seal regime, and the newly defined speed range where the water-entry interactions exhibit distinct behavior, waiting to be explored in future research efforts. The speed range examined in this study, between 10 and 30 meters per second, is particularly significant, as it is the speed range most commonly experienced in real-world scenarios, such as in the context of underwater explosions. A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory. The $\theta$-terms also lead to the formation of quark-antiquark condensates in a state of dyonic hair, potentially erasing another universal symmetry, thereby allowing the effective theory to incorporate both hybrd and dyonic states within its range. The resulting effective action no longer includes a Weyl anomaly, as the $\theta$-terms cause the axion fields to be driven to a point of mass equality with the dyonic charged states. Consequently, the range of universal symmetries is limited to those which can be part of the effective action defined by the low-energy, point-like behavior of the dyonic charged states. The effective action itself becomes a Witten-like effect arising from the $\theta$-terms, and which can be interpreted as a non-trivial, topologically-robust, generalized Witten effect. The range of universal symmetries in the effective theories we studied is found to be restricted to those which can be part of the Witten-like effects generated from the $\theta$-terms. The outcome of this research implies that the hypothesis that quantum gravity must be devoid of universal symmetries is too vague, and thus we propose a more precise statement: any universal symmetry in the effective theories of IIB supergravity is neither born nor immortal, but rather dies from shock due to its own emergence. The range of its charged states, however, remains immortal, as it is defined by the monodromy transformation near which the moduli space is established, and which forms the boundary of its effective theory. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun. The successful generation of multi-phonon packages can be refined by fine-tuning the quantum dot's coupling to the acoustic cavity and modifying the laser drive, leading to an expansion of the phonon number range, even in the presence of decoherence within the quantum dot. The findings presented in this research can be applied to a wide variety of acoustic resonators, both free-space and enclosed, and showcase the quantum dot's role as a phonon gun, offering a promising solution for phonon number selection with precision. The development of this system also paves the way for the creation of a superposition of N-phonon packages in an acoustic cavity, a phenomenon with potential applications in quantum metrology. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. This work is an initial step towards developing and evaluating methods for predicting a wide range of chemical properties in polymers, filling a significant gap in the current literature. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation. Our dataset is accessible upon request from the corresponding author. Our model's potential for real-world applications is highlighted by its performance on long, curved structures with low contrast, making it a suitable foundation for developing automated analysis of CT scans in other clinical settings. Our code and dataset have the potential to contribute to the development of other networks based on the Unet architecture, attention mechanisms, and dense blocks. Our dataset can be used as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of other esophageal tumor segmentation models. Our model's reliability in real-world clinical scenarios is supported by its consistency across repeated studies, its ability to accurately identify the extent of tumors even in difficult-to-reach parts of the esophagus, and its ability to differentiate between tumors and adjacent structures with air pockets or feeding tubes. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. In areas where there is strong adherence to norms, we observed decreased dissemination of misinformation. In contrast, in areas lacking in conscientiousness, we found that the effects of local culture on misinformation spread were more significant than the effects of state-level conditions. Our research reveals the substantial influence of geographical factors on online misinformation dissemination in one notable social media context, suggesting its broad applicability to other online environments. Our study highlights the importance of considering the broader social context of information diffusion to prevent the spread of misinformation. Our approach and findings can be utilized to develop predictive models of online misinformation dissemination and evaluate the effectiveness of anti-disinformation initiatives. Our research identifies potential policy interventions, such as promoting civic education and cultivating a sense of community in local areas, to combat the spread of online misinformation. Our study's empirical framework can be applied to the study of other information phenomena spread online. Our analysis demonstrates the value of integrating large data sets with theoretical models in understanding complex phenomena of of this kind. Our approach can be repurposed for the analysis of other large data sets combining both geographical and social elements. Our research provides a useful contribution to the fields of sociology, politics, and economics studying online behavior, and to the broader scientific community interested in the study of information diffusion. Our study's empirical findings, approaches, and analysis can be applied to various other contexts beyond the specific case study presented. Our approach and methodology are suitable for the investigation of other complex phenomena characterized by both geographical and social factors. Our research offers a significant empirical contribution to the understanding of online behavior in the United States, and provides a valuable methodology for investigative research into other complex phenomena characterized by both geographical and social elements. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. To address these challenges, we propose introducing a degree of semantic flexibility, which we demonstrate can be achieved through the application of fuzzy sets and similarity metrics. Furthermore, we present a conceptual framework for our automated testing system, which incorporates a set of basic testing scenarios, a natural language similarity assessment module, and a generator for random test cases. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to the development of an automated testing system for conversational systems that is both practical and theoretically sound. This paper is an extension of our previous work presented at the 2023 Congress of the Italian Association for Artificial Intelligence. It incorporates additional challenges faced in testing conversational systems and offers a more comprehensive framework for our research. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ChengHaoLi/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The advantages of this approach are most visibly demonstrated when formulating and solving certain stochastic optimization problems. The implementation details, methodology, and notable results from Hypatia are openly available on GitHub, alongside the Julia package itself. The approach presented in this work offers valuable insights into the formulation and solving of various optimization applications, as well as the benefits of using Julia as a backend for high-performance computational tasks. The methodology behind Hypatia has been found to yield efficient results for a range of stochastic optimization problems, including a novel application of the multi-scale stochastic subgradient method. The code for Hypatia is listed as an exemplary implementation of how to efficiently define and solve certain types of convex optimization problems using Julia and JuMP. The approach described in this work aligns with the broader strategy of developing specialized solvers that can be combined with general-purpose optimization frameworks. The most notable benefit of this approach is the opportunity to reuse existing solver infrastructure, thereby eliminating the need for the manual definition of sensitive mathematical objects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. Consequently, our recommendations emphasize incorporating MRIQC features without preprocessing into quality control pipelines, while highlighting the necessity for careful consideration when generalizing models to newly acquired, previously unseen data. This is because, despite advancements in machine learning, models trained on diverse, complex datasets with varying population characteristics still struggle with true generalizability. This implies that, even with enhanced models, careful examination of site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities will continue to be crucial for informed decision-making in quality control decisions. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks. Our research provides a foundational step towards exploring more complex and dynamic phenomena, with implications for managing and securing future transportation and energy infrastructure. With private EVs becoming increasingly prevalent, it is essential to consider their impact on the grid, especially in areas with high penetration of renewable energy, where the relationship between transportation and energy systems becomes more interdependent. Our work highlights the need for a comprehensive, integrated framework that accounts for both transportation and energy dynamics, especially when evaluating policies for private EV management, given the potential for tailored strategies that consider both environmental and operational benefits, as well as potential conflicts with existing grid infrastructure and resources. By examining various scenarios, we found that incentivizing optimal charging schedules can reduce grid losses and accelerate recovery in the aftermath of an outage, whereas considering the grid condition can help manage EV adoption in a way that balances the benefits of reduced energy losses with the costs of delaying their adoption. Our approach and the resulting policy insights can be applied to various contexts, including those with existing power grid and transportation management frameworks, by incorporating the additional private EV-related objectives and constraints into the existing optimization problems through efficient algorithmic techniques, with the potential to enhance grid resilience and recovery through targeted private EV policies, with implications for practicing engineers and policymakers. With the increasing complexity of power and transportation networks, it is crucial to explore more advanced and dynamic models that account for varied private EV ownership patterns, grid conditions, and transportation demands, as well as the impact of driver behavior on EV performance, to ensure that policies for private EV management prioritize grid resilience, recovery, and operation in the face of outages and normal operating conditions. Our research provides a foundational step towards this goal, with the potential to contribute to ongoing policy debates, while also facilitating further, more comprehensive analyses of private EVs within integrated power and transportation networks. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Utilizing this approach, we reanalyzed the Hubble diagram for 24 super-luminous SN Ia observations from the Pannhauser survey and the Candels & SNe IIIa sample, and discovered that the lens-induced additional scattering in SN Ia magnitudes could be as small as $0.035$ magnitudes at $z \approx 1.5$, though this value requires confirmation through larger SN Ia datasets. Nonetheless, this study demonstrates the feasibility of recovering galactic halo density information from SN Ia data and suggests that future SN Ia missions will be capable of accurately determining the mass-to-light ratio of the local universe with a precision of $10\%$, primarily through the analysis of SN Ia photometry rather than their light curves. This research also highlights the promise of combining SN Ia data with galaxy weak lensingconvergence to gain a deeper understanding of the distribution of matter density within galactic haloes. Ultimately, this work will serve as a foundation for the design of future SN Ia missions that can simultaneously investigate the cosmological parameters of the $\Lambda$CDM model and the distribution of matter within the local universe. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. As a result, we have a functional, medium-loss per photon, 10 Gbit/s capable device that can serve as a reliable source of single photons for quantum communication networks. Furthermore, this technique's versatility allows for the generation of entangled photon pairs via double quantum dot structure based on a modified Tetrahedral layout. The successful creation of high T center densities within the confines of a 220nm device layer layer, paired with the presence of suitable spectral diffusion levels, makes this silicon-based approach an attractive solution for mid-bandwidth, high-fidelity quantum communication applications. The developed technique also has the potential to be scaled up to newer generation SOI wafers with deeper device layers. The robust nature of this approach is underlined by the findings of a comprehensive reliability test, where there were no substantial changes in spin-dependent optical transitions or spectral diffusion over extended periods of time. The technological advancements outlined in this research demonstrate the feasibility of efficient and reliable T center-based silicon devices, capable of maintaining their performance even in the presence of fabrication variations and environmental stress. The developed technology's scalability, coupled with the inherent benefits of silicon-based platforms, positions it favorably for the development of large-scale, reliable quantum communication networks. The technique described herein also offers a promising solution for the generation of entangled photon pairs in small-scale devices. The extensive reliability findings from this research will contribute to a better understanding of the robustness of T type damage centers in silicon. The developed technology has the potential to be seamlessly integrated with existing silicon-based quantum processing units (QPU) and silicon photonic devices, due to its compatibility with standard CMOS processing techniques. We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous outcomes for matrix-valued settings as seen in recent estimates by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. For functions under SRP we establish stronger inequalities of a Bernstein-type for matrix-valued functions, thereby broadening earlier general bounds for linear combinations of positive definite matrices due to Kyng and Song.

Furthermore, we investigate the unique case where we condition on Bernoulli random variables with independent outcomes for their sum. In doing so, we establish sharpened estimates resulting in specifically tailored log-Sobolev inequalities, as well as Talagrand's convex distance inequality, with concentration inequalities for convex functions, polynomials, and matrix-valued functions as direct consequences. These generalised inequalities encompass results for uniform distributions over discrete slices of the cube, extensively explored in numerous studies. The current approach builds upon recent outcomes from Hermon and Salez as well as on a broader framework involving modified log-Sobolev inequalities within the context of the discrete cube, with independent utility of its own. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Furthermore, Springer demonstrated that the process of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K) can be viewed as a refinement of the classification system employed by the special orthogonal group SO_n(K), with conjugacy classes in the symplectic group Sp_n(K) being made up of conjugacy classes within the special orthogonal group SO_2n-1(K) that share the same characteristics. Van der Kallen's translation of Springer's work includes an additional appendix containing research conducted by himself and T.A. Springer on the topic of conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K). The translation was originally published in the Springer Proceedings in Mathematics/Kioto Series volume 18 in 2010. The research presented in the appendix builds upon Springer's findings by examining fields K that have a characteristic other than two and three, and provides an updated comprehension of conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K). Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Ultimately, our findings illustrate the value of early transplant attempts with incompatible donors, and the potential benefits of combining transplantation and desensitization treatments, which can be achieved by following a threshold strategy. Finally, our research offers policymakers a framework for evaluating strategic transplant policies that consider incompatibility, desensitization, and reticulation treatments, and provides insights into how to develop policies that prioritize transplants with lower levels of incompatibility. Firms and organizations involved in kidney transplantation and desensitization services can use our model to optimize their treatments and measure the effectiveness of combining these services. Our study can also be applied to other transplant scenarios involving incompatible donors and recipients. We conclude by highlighting the scarcity of research focusing on transplant decision-making and encourage future investigators to explore issues such as how to incorporate ethics into decision-making, how to handle multiple criteria evaluation, and how to address uncertainty regarding incompatibility. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for the widespread applications of word2vec embeddings, while our empirical analysis also offers insights into their capabilities and limitations when employed on complex, dynamic text corpora. Our code is available at https://github.com/haixiaoqi/math-nlp. Our financial dataset is based on a subset of the data analyzed in our related work, available at https://github.com/haixiaoqi/polar-word-sim. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Furthermore, we've developed a non-linear mobility model to simulate the interaction of the interface with itself, previously missing in numerical solutions to the Stefan problem. The resulting method and examples illustrate the capabilities of this new technique. The associated software, known as Biot2, is a part of the Geben framework and features open-source code available online. This work paves the way for further development of the Biot2 framework in modeling complex fluid interactions with changing phases. The results presented here have been previously published in various studies, including those found in Physical Review E, Journal of Computational Physics, and Journal of Fluid Mechanics. The numerical strategy described in this research has been utilized to solve a variety of problems, including the melting boundary problem, the growth of dendrites, the Rayleigh--B\'enard instability, the motion of an interface in a channel, and the formation of Landau lesions. The software developed here has been used to create animated visualizations of these simulations, which are also available online. The research discussed in this article was supported by the National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, and the National Institute of Environmental Sciences. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research extends previous findings, extending the rationalizable setting to more general contexts of games with general payoff matrices and multiple equilibria, and, in contrast to prior work, without the need for an exponentially large number of samples. Our most efficient algorithm extends the current benchmark established in 2021 to a wider range of games, while our theories and techniques provide a framework for understanding the relationship between rationalizable learning and the presence of correlated equilibria. This framework enables the derivation of an optimal sample size that scales polynomially in line with problem parameters, offering a significant improvement over the existing benchmark set in 2021 and extending the boundaries of games that can be learned relative to previous limitations established in 2021. This research paves the way for further study into the efficient learning of other generalizable settings of multiplayer games. It is demonstrated in the experiments that our algorithms are capable of handling practical scenarios consisting of multiple players with complex dynamics, demonstrating the practical viability of learning rationalizable behavior in these contexts. This research builds upon the cutting-edge results established in 2021, extending the scope of learnable games to a broader class of context, and, in contrast to prior work, without the requirement for an exponentially large number of samples. This extension is made possible by the integration of innovative techniques that, beyond the discovery of a rationalizable action profile, also ensure the absence of (swap-)regret through the adoption of a correlated exploration strategy and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering additional value as standalone contributions.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach based on a lightweight, general-purpose PDF fitting framework called 'UnPDF', which can seamlessly combine diverse sets of PDF predictions, including those already fitted to experimental data, across various processes and scattering regimes. UnPDF leverages a distributed architecture to automate the incorporation of PDF predictions, including the application of relevant evolution equations, and features a user-friendly interface to facilitate easy adoption for potential users. By providing a versatile platform, we demonstrate that UnPDF can be readily used as a foundation for fitting PDF candidates to real-world experimental data, while offering a marked increase in efficiency by minimizing redundant calculations. Additionally, UnPDF includes multiple features such as a modular design, support for multiple PDF formats, and automated integrity checking to ensure accurate results. By making UnPDF an open-source tool, we are confident that it will facilitate streamlined PDF fitting processes for research groups worldwide. The proposed framework is particularly suited for fitting PDF candidates in the context of hadron colliders, yet due to the universal nature of UnPDF, it can be applied to fitting PDFs for other particle scattering experiments involving deep inelastic scattering off nucleons, nuclei, or other probes. The accompanying code for UnPDF is available at https://github.com/PDF-fitters/UnPDF. The detailed documentation for UnPDF, along with example use cases, is available at https://unpdf.readthedocs.io/. The derived results from the presented study are actionable and can be reproduced by downloading the accompanying dataset from https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/6QGK3Q. The relevant research papers were published in Physical Review D 105, 074005 and Physical Review D 105, 074006. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. When applied to a range of challenging tasks, it yields superior results and extends the range of valid learning rates. The code is available at https://github.com/ghyi/VRED. The variance reduction based experience replay framework can be used in various settings, including those with time-varying system parameters, multiple learning rates, and sample curious episodes. The study provides a practical solution to the problem of varying reward functions over time, an issue that affects many real-world systems and benchmarks, such as traffic flow, financial markets, and game environments with changing reward structures. The simplest implementation of the variance reduction based experience replay framework maintains the lowest computational demands while offering a significant improvement in policy optimization in dynamic systems, outperforming the standard experience replay method by up to 10 times in some cases. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We refer to these as multiple ISE (imaginary Schramm-Loewner evolution) and its associated multiple IWAM (imaginary Williams-Briggs process). We establish that multiple ISE and its associated multiple IWAM can be realized on the upper half-plane and the first orthant by evolving multiple SLE on their boundary. We also discover that the statistical properties of the multiple ISE and its associated multiple IWAM are entirely determined by the underlying Dyson model or Bru-Wishart process. We interpret these findings as multiple ISE and its associated multiple IWAM being natural generalizations of the process that evolves the 1D SLE boundary, the 1D SLE trace, and the 1D SLE length, which are all entirely determined by a single SLE evolving in time on the real line. We also establish that multiple ISE can be realized on any domain that evolves in time and has the property that its boundary evolves in time according to the Dyson model, with associated multiple IWAM on the interior of the domain. We refer to this process as imaginary Schramm-Loewner evolution on a random domain, or ISLED for short. This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. Finally, the response of the jet flame to acoustic vibrations was found to be more significant at the flame base, where reaction rate oscillations are most susceptible to the disruption caused by vortex rings. This study demonstrates the necessity of considering reaction rate oscillations caused by the breakdown of Kelvin-Helmholtzt vortex rings within jet flames when analyzing their response to acoustic vibrations. It also highlights the suitability of combining LES with RANS models to capture the average and fluctuating properties of jet flames. Finally, it shows that the tips of vortex rings are the primary source of flame noise resulting from acoustic vibrations, while the rings' breakdown causes reaction rate fluctuations that lead to instability in flames. This knowledge can be leveraged to develop noise-reducing technologies for flame engines used in aircraft propulsion systems. This research also contributes a linear model of a jet flame reacting to acoustic vibrations that can be utilized in the design of combustion chambers to minimize flame noise. This is particularly important for the development of future low-emission aircraft engines used in long-haul flights. This study was conducted as part of a larger project aimed at developing a nonlinear model of a jet flame reacting to acoustic vibrations, which will enable the design of combustion chambers that minimize flame noise caused by vortex-ring instability. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, our approach has helped in identifying novel biological mechanisms associated with certain conditions, such as an association between type 2 diabetes and SNPs that target certain histone modification patterns specifically within pancreatic iscell types. Our approach has been made publicly available as a web-based tool, enabling users to explore the functional aspects of trait-associated SNPs and guide subsequent experimental studies. Our findings and approach provide a framework for elucidating the complex mechanisms underlying human traits and conditions by examining the influence of non-coding SNPs on gene expression and other cellular processes. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. The implication is that the majority of the stellar mass compact objects within the Milky Way are actually neutron stars rather than black holes. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to modify the standard generative modeling approach by integrating an auxiliary diversity-aware task that predicts the degree of semantic variety for each response. This variety-aware approach was put to use on both single-goal and multi-goal conversational generation settings. Experimental results across two datasets revealed a significant improvement in Natural Language Inference Diversity, as well as evaluators' preferences for responses in real-world conversations. This variety-aware approach's effectiveness was also validated through ablation tests. This study's findings are expected to contribute to the development of neural conversational agents that produce more semantically diverse responses. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/zhuyong2016/NLIDiversity. This study's findings are also relevant to the evaluation and improvement of semantic variety in conversations generated by other approaches. This research's code can be utilized as a baseline for comparing various diversity-enhancing conversational generation methods. This study's assessment metric and variety-aware approach may serve as guidelines for developing more effective methods to enhance the semantic variety of responses in casual conversations. This variety-aware approach's applicability extends to multiple goal conversational generation settings, making it a viable solution for real-world applications involving conversational generation. This research's limitations, potential future work, and additional experimental results are discussed in the appendix of this paper. The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. In both cases, we examined the boundaries of which stars could maintain hydrogen burning, taking into account factors like mass loss rates and spin-down times. Although the occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning was delayed with rotation, we found that it could still happen in stars with masses as low as 0.7 times the mass of the sun. This limit could be further lowered to 0.65 solar masses, however this would require a longer spin-down time or less mass loss during the spin-down phase. This research suggests that very low-mass stars in the hydrogen burning branch of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram might have formed in binary systems where the low-mass star is accreting material from a companion star. If this is the case, we can expect the occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning to be less common among these stars due to their likely higher spin-down time and mass loss during the spin-down phase. This could provide an explanation for the observed deficit of these stars in the hydrogen burning branch. This research was also applied to model the development of brown dwarfs in binary systems where the low-mass star is undergoing mass transfer. In this scenario, we found that while the spin-induced break-up limit leads to mass loss and shrinkage, the star might still experience sustainable hydrogen burning before it reaches the 0.45 solar mass kissing point, where it ceases to burn hydrogen and instead experience helium burning. This could provide an explanation for the observed deficiency of very low-mass stars in the helium burning branch of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. In this paper, an algorithm is described that can tackle this problem by breaking a maximum allowed number of nodes, which is indicative of a common real-world scenario, and includes an explicit node-splitting variant for bipartite graphs. A theoretical analysis of the algorithm's time and node-breaking complexity has been provided, along with an illustrative example, and a node-splitting variant example for bipartite graphs. The code associated with this research is available online. The approach presented can serve as a foundation for future research aimed at exploring additional visualization properties. The approach was tested on real-world data sets resulting in visually interpretable graphs. The code utilized in this research has been made publicly accessible. A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  To further evaluate the technique, metrics for side-channel leakage were proposed, which demonstrated that HyperDegrade could be effective in side-channel amplification without compromising data integrity.  A fair comparison between three different performance degradation strategies in combination with Flush+Reload attacks revealed HyperDegrade's efficacy, which enabled the development of an attack on an OpenSSL vulnerability three times more efficient than other methods.  In addition, HyperDegrade's applicability to Raccoon-like attacks was also demonstrated, which can succeed with real-world data and extend the scope of existing attacks to various protocols, filling in the gap left by previous research.  A feasible approach to countermeasures was also explored through the application of HyperDegrade to a mock scenario of an attack on a real-world target, which highlighted the importance of considering the interplay between a program's behavior and cache evictions.  In light of these findings, it is recommended that future research into side-channel attacks and countermeasures also account for the effects of cache evictions on the system. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA. In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options. It has been demonstrated that this method accurately represents a linear strategy profile and can be effective in achieving a cooperative equilibrium through learning. The advantages and limitations of this method have been examined in comparison to other established approaches. A system of multiple agents that cooperate through a complex network has been modeled, and it has been shown that the shortest path to a cooperative equilibrium is equal to the degree of the most sparsely connected agent. Finally, it has been found that learning from the most advantageous action in each state can be a reliable strategy in the presence of an agent's own uncertainty as well as the uncertainty of the other agents. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method. Interestingly, our method was found to consistently outperform RFF on multiple machine learning tasks, using both real-world and generated data sets. In addition to its efficiency, this method also demonstrates the ability to improve the classification performance on various datasets, notably those that are previously difficult to classify with kernel-based methods. In particular, our method was found to yield notable improvements when applied to both cancer subtype classification using microarray data and the classification of MNIST digits. In summary, this paper presents a novel and superior method of kernel approximation that is both computationally efficient and offers enhanced performance, making it a valuable contribution to the machine learning community. In contrast to the limitations of existing methods, this new approach provably minimizes the number of required features while maintaining the desired level of accuracy, thereby enabling the seamless integration of kernel-based techniques into large-scale learning applications. In addition, this paper provides a detailed analysis of the associated computational costs and offers practical guidelines for optimizing parameter settings in order to balance both the number of features and the associated computational expenses in different applications. In order to facilitate widespread adoption, this method is made available as a user-friendly kernel approximation tool, accessible from https://kyrrs.github.io/kappax/. In order to validate the robustness and reliability of this new method, this paper also reports on multiple negative control experiments involving both artificial and real-world data sets. Ultimately, this paper is aimed at a broad audience of machine learning researchers and practitioners working on kernel-based methods and related applications, including but not limited to cancer subtype classification using microarray data, image recognition, and natural language processing. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. Despite the benefits of this design, we discovered that the necessary duration becomes excessively long for larger chains of ions. A modified version of the Molmer-Sorensen gate is then proposed, incorporating a higher frequency that prioritizes faster execution over frequency robustness, or a combination of both properties, depending on the specific application. A demonstration of this new gate design is performed on a chain of three ions, showing that it can entertain a wide range of frequencies, extending from two kilohertz to twenty kilohertz, with minimal decline in precision. A numerical analysis of this modified gate is then conducted on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions, showing that the necessary duration is significantly reduced while maintaining an average decline of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation. This new gate design demonstrates considerable frequency robustness, maintaining an average decline of under five percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation for chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions, and is thus considered an efficient and versatile method for creating quantum gates involving trapped ions. Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid electronic theory's strongly correlated systems and graphene, yet the $sp^{2}$-electrons that form Dirac bands in graphene lack strong interactions. Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. We propose GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ as a new material where Dirac electrons are paired with strong interactions and frustrated magnetism. Calculations indicate its crystallographic and electronic properties harbor symmetry-protected Dirac points at the Fermi level, allowing for multifaceted physics encompassing possible instabilities of charge, magnetism, or superconductivity. By merging various methods to assess its many-body behavior, researchers have observed potential transitions to Mott-Hubbard, magnetic or charge ordering states, along with $f$-wave unconventional superconductivity in this unique compound. Thus, GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ is an extraordinary example where the confluence of strong correlations, frustrated magnetism, and unusual band structure creates an 'ideal laboratory' for the emergence of novel, possibly robust phenomena. It is anticipated that this new material will play a significant role in the ongoing quest to understand complex electronic phases of matter. In light of this, further experimental verification of the predicted robust electronic phases in GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ through, e.g., transport, magnetic and NMR-scattering studies is highly recommended. In conclusion, the extraordinary band structure of GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ makes it an 'electronic holy grail' worthy of in-depth investigation. In addition, this compound belongs to a broader class of 3d transition metal compounds with strong interactions and diverse possible ground states, deemed 'Dirac materials with strong correlations'. Ultimately, this category is seen as a promising source of novel and potentially robust electronic phases that can result from the interplay between strong interactions, frustrated magnetism and unusual band structures. In this context, determining the ground state of GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ through both theoretical and experimental studies is seen as crucial for understanding the intricate relationship between electronic phases, interatomic interactions and lattice complexity. In this regard, researchers propose considering it as a'model material' for understanding the complex relationship between strong interactions, magnetic frustration, unusual band structures and the resulting diverse possible ground states

Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach generates plausible face variations from a given image, which we demonstrate through both two-dimensional and three-dimensional visualization methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/SADRNet.

This investigation seeks to examine the capabilities of Informed OCR (iOCR) in accurately capturing vote tabulation data, as the system is designed with an advanced spell-checking feature to correct common errors associated with traditional OCR technology, which the research reveals results in iOCR outperforming traditional OCR methods. To determine the effectiveness of iOCR in this context, a statistical analysis was conducted of 500 vote count reports from a recent election in the United States, representing over 3.5 million votes. The study compared the accuracy of iOCR and the leading traditional OCR solution, Tesseract, in processing these reports. The findings showed that iOCR demonstrated a 29.6% higher accuracy rate than Tesseract, with a particularly notable 41.1% improvement in correcting transposition errors commonly observed in vote tabulation data. Consequently, the research confirms that iOCR is a more reliable option than Tesseract for processing this type of data. Nonetheless, the study also uncovered an 11.8% error rate associated with iOCR, suggesting that human review is still necessary to ensure the flawless capture of vote tabulation data. Ultimately, the results of this research are expected to be beneficial to election administrators and researchers worldwide who strive to improve the accuracy of vote count reporting. The proposed approach can be applied to a broader spectrum of tabular documents involving numerical data. The study's findings are pertinent to anyone seeking to automate the extraction of numerical information from documents with similar structures to vote tabulations.
