This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. This technique enables us to apply existing asymptotic results from related problems. The sum and maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations can then be analyzed by applying recent findings by Birkner, Greven, and Barraes to a modified version of the conditioned random walk. The rates for $k_n$ that yield asymptotic independence and identity distribution can be determined by examining the limiting behavior of the conditioned random walk itself. The achievements of this work also include derived moment and extreme value distribution asymptotic results for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ randomly generated uniform parking locations of size $n$, for two distinct distance metrics. The findings of this work can be viewed as extending previous research by Diaconis and Hicks along with providing a detailed explanation of the underlying mechanisms governing the asymptotic behavior of parking distributions. The relationship between the distance metrics and the parameters of the random walk can be explored in more depth, thereby shedding light on the conditions that guarantee asymptotic independence and identity distribution of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The investigation reveals that the periodic variations of the critical voltage threshold can be described by an interplay of quantum interference, capacitance, and the discrete nature of the junctions, and may serve as a manifestation of quantum fluctuations within Josephson junctions. The study also uncovers the potential for precise control over quantum phase slips and suggests that nanowires could be used in quantum simulations and other applications. The research utilizes a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental measurements to interpret the findings, and the utility of the investigation is enhanced by an open-source code for solving the phase-dependent capacitance of Josephson junctions. The work is further enriched by an accompanying demonstration of a quantum circuit that can be employed to investigate the behavior of quantum phase slips. Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengzw/NovelViewPrediction. Our model's effectiveness is attributed to a specially designed two-component representation, a spatial attention mechanism, and the inclusion of motion information through optical flow, leading to a significant improvement in predicted video quality. Our approach has numerous applications, such as enhancing novel view video generation for 3D virtual avatars and enhancing realism in 3D reconstructions. Our model's versatility is demonstrated by conducting quantitative and qualitative analyses on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, showing its ability to generalize to unseen data, produce high-quality predictions, and exhibit robustness in video predictions spanning wider angles of 45 degrees. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. In evaluating the reliability of the 'well mixed' model, our analysis raises important concerns about the accuracy of predictions obtained using this model, particularly in regards to its assumption of uniform aerosol particle distribution. In contrast, the non-uniform distribution of aerosol particles observed in our study suggests that the 'well mixed' model significantly overestimates the transmission risk in bus environments. In light of these findings, we advocate for the use of more realistic, spatial models of aerosol transport in bus settings to better inform strategies for mitigating the spread of airborne transmitted diseases. In such scenarios, where the distance between individuals is generally greater than the aerosol particle mean free path, the 'well mixed' model is no longer considered valid and may even inaccurately predict transmission risks that are instead low, due to the incompatibility of bus confinement with 'well mixed' conditions. In such environments, targeted interventions aimed at reducing transmission risk through the disruption of aerosol particle clustering and the promotion of particle settling, may significantly improve public health outcomes. In bus settings, this could be achieved by adjusting seat arrangements to facilitate shorter distance interactions between individuals and/or implementing measures that accelerate aerosol particle deposition onto surfaces and within lower respiratory tract compartments. In evaluating the effectiveness of these interventions in bus environments, it is essential to utilize models that accurately capture the complex dynamics of aerosol transport. In the absence of such models, our analysis provides a detailed, quantitative framework for evaluating bus ventilation conditions in relation to the spread of airborne transmitted diseases. In this context, key factors that influence the transport of virus-laden aerosols in enclosed spaces are summarized in a table that is relevant to a broader range of settings beyond urban buses. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. Additionally, the investigation revealed that the Bismuth layers induce a magnetic impurity effect on the Cobalt layers, which could also contribute to the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect. Nonetheless, the magnitude of this effect appears too small to influence the Ferromagnetic Cobalt's magnetization. Consequently, the study proposes that the Magneto-Optical Kerr Effect be used in conjunction with transport measurements when investigating the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in magnetic multilayers. In conclusion, the investigation demonstrated that the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect can result from elastic scattering of free carriers by rough interfaces and crystallographic misfits between layers with different crystal structures. Nonetheless, the magnitude of this effect depends on the compatibility of the layers' crystal structures and can be manipulated by engineering interfacial sites of carrier scattering. The research also highlighted the potential applications of Bismuth in modifying the Anomalous Hall effect and Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity in transition metal layers. The findings are relevant to the development of novel magnetic and superconductor systems, such as LaAlO3/SrTiO3 and graphene, which can be modified by incorporating Bismuth layers. The study presented here may serve as a foundation for the investigation of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in other compatible layer pairs. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's generalisation performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We believe that our methodology provides a valuable foundation for developing new training algorithms focused on ensuring a neural network's stability and robustness. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Despite the complexity of these calculations, the code can generate precise results with a reasonable computational time, making it a valuable resource for theoretical physicists and experimental researchers alike. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. Furthermore, the proposed framework demonstrates improved performance in PET images reconstructed from various OOD scenarios, such as different MRI acquisition parameters, expression levels of target proteins, and various tumors, compared to a benchmark model relying solely on learned invariance. This approach provides a promising solution for tackling various challenges associated with PET scans, particularly those involving sensitive populations where reducing radiation exposure is crucial. The proposed framework's code is available at https://github.com/zhengjy/AUDINET-PET-Reconstruction. The code can be utilized for reproducing the results presented in this study, as well as serving as a foundation for future research aimed at improving PET imaging, particularly in sensitive populations requiring frequent imaging, such as young individuals. The potential of this novel neural network framework has been demonstrated in standard PET reconstructions, and its applicability to other deep learning models and various applications has been highlighted. Nonetheless, future research is necessary to thoroughly explore this framework's versatility and potential drawbacks. A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. However, the study also finds that the underlying ideas of CT are not sufficient to capture the connections within the text and that the computer systems already incorporate the required information. Therefore, the study concludes that CT's primary value lies in its ability to analyze the coherence of conversations rather than providing the underlying connections. This implies that the underlying connections within the text are primarily determined by the relationships between successive statements and are not governed by a set of fixed rules. This study was previously published as part of the 2017 conference proceedings of the Association for Computational Linguistics. The revised version incorporates additional analysis and clarifications based on feedback from conference attendees. The original research paper can be found in the ACL 2017 repository, the CT and QCT models are available in the CT4MATL repository, and the annotated datasets are accessible in the Centering Corpora Repository. The issue with the QCT model's evaluation metric has been resolved in the revised version. The study's methodology has been updated to address clarifications raised by researchers. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets. The most effective model obtained across all evaluations was subsequently utilized as a benchmark for an in-depth analysis of the factors influencing geospatial distance estimation, including the characteristics of the datasets used and the results of previous research discussed in the literature. To facilitate reproducibility and further research, the models developed, along with the code and datasets used, are available for public access through GitHub repositories. The approaches and results presented in this research provide valuable insights for academics and industry professionals alike who are interested in indoor positioning technologies. The novel machine learning-based approach proposed in this research offers a versatile and adaptable solution with universal applicability to a wide range of indoor environments. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Additionally, this research reveals that varying RF cavity fill levels can also affect beam breakup threshold, offering another design variable to optimize machine performance. Finally, considerations are presented for future energy recovery linac designs aiming to minimize beam breakup instability and realize the full potential of energy recovery technology. The beam-RF interaction simulation tool developed during this study can be utilized for evaluating and optimizing the performance of various energy recovery configurations. The findings discussed herein provide a foundation for further investigation into multi-pass energy recovery schemes and other particle accelerators influenced by beam-RF interaction effects. The associated beam-RF interaction simulation code has been made available for the community to use and further develop at https://github.com/wangzhenphd/BIC. The design of modern energy recovery linacs is characterized by the need to maximize beam current, recycle as much energy as possible from spent beam, and minimize the number of passes required to achieve this goal. However, the energy loss per particle remains relatively low in linear accelerators, meaning that a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. As a result, the beam breakup instability poses a significant challenge. The minimum beam current required to maintain stability is defined as the threshold current. It is crucial to note that the actual beam current in practice must be significantly higher than the threshold current to ensure that the beam remains stable throughout its entire journey. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. By contrast, in the NMRK limit, the two-gluon CEV resists such decomposition, thereby illustrating the greater complexity encountered when considering scenarios beyond the MRK kinematic limit. In such cases, even within a NMRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV cannot be accounted for by a single color component, demonstrating that the BFKL equation necessitates inclusion of color triple Casimir operators at the NNLL accuracy level. In addition, calculations were also performed for a one-loop seven-gluon configuration known as the 'daisy' topology, yielding a one-loop 'daisy' CEV for two gluons with additional emitters in a rapidity-offshell configuration. Although this result is specific to the NMRK kinematic limit, the corresponding two-gluon CEV was found to be comparable in magnitude to its six-gluon amplitude counterpart. In this work, the dispersion relation of the BFKL gluon trajectory was also investigated in the NMRK kinematic limit, revealing that even in the presence of a one-loop 'daisy' CEV, the BFKL gluon trajectory remains essentially unchanged. By contrast, contributions from CEVs with higher multiplicities become significant at higher energies, leading to an enhancement of the BFKL gluon trajectory with energy. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. By incorporating the effects of surface curvature on the free energy of stretching brushes, we discover a universal scaling rule applicable to all curved brush configurations. This study provides a fundamental understanding of the intricate relationships between curved surface geometry, molecular chain behavior, and free energy calculations, offering a theoretical framework for a wide range of block copolymer melt scenarios. The scalable nature of this research also enables the development of a brush geometry simulator based on various curved surfaces, facilitating the exploration of block copolymer melt assembly via the strong-stretching theory. The limitations of the strong-stretching approximation are discussed in the conclusion, along with the potential advantages of incorporating the effects of surface curvature on polymer brush geometry into the simulation of block copolymer melt assembly via the strong-stretching theory. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. It's straightforward to see that the larger a graph gets the more its metric dimension will increase, but we're interested in finding patterns where this isn't true. Two examples of graphs that follow this pattern are closed trees and power grids, for which we're able to find formulas that show they have a linear metric dimension when the number of vertices is very large. On the other hand, we've discovered that both random graphs and certain types of geometric graphs have a metric dimension that grows in a different way - specifically, it increases in proportion to the square root of the number of vertices, when that number is very large. But interestingly, adding a random edge to an empty graph will sometimes increase the metric dimension, with the probability of that happening being directly proportional to the square of the number of vertices raised to the power of -1.5, when that number of vertices is very large. Finally, we've considered the problem of finding the minimum identifying set of a graph as a problem worth solving, and came up with an algorithm that can do this for any graph, but in the process discovered that it creates a stack of problems that are all essentially the same as the original, but with the advantage that each one has a smaller metric dimension than the last - meaning that we can find the minimum identifying set of the original graph by looking at all the possible sets of points that are a certain distance from each other and seeing which one is smallest, where the size of that distance is the k value we're looking for. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Despite the need for regular retraining to account for changing source spectra, this method provides a robust means of enhancing the detail retained in processed images, retaining up to 95% of the information lost during compression to 64 bits. This demonstrates the machine learning-based method's potential to improve a wide range of galaxy-wide analysis tasks by retaining the essential features of large-scale image patterns. This work paves the way for further optimizing the models through better handling of time series and multiple map analysis. This approach can be extended to other space missions, like the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer, that produce high-quality images from extensive observations, and it may also be applicable to other fields like medical imaging. This research is particularly relevant to the community studying gamma-ray emissions from the Milky Way. This work is part of an broader initiative, the Machine Learning Space Physics Laboratory, that aims to leverage the power of machine learning for space weather prediction, satellite performance optimization, and the analysis of physical phenomena from space plasma to gamma-ray observations. This work is a result of collaborations within the initiative and contributes a concrete application of machine learning for the benefit of the space physics community. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We test this metric on various optimization domains and find that it is significantly lower for domains with specific properties such as being submodular. We conclude that the serial dictatorship mechanism is a versatile and effective tool with a broad range of applications in group decision-making, often resulting in fair and robust outcomes that prioritize honesty. We hope this study will guide further research into the efficiency of combinatorial optimization domains by examining the complexity of the price of serial dictatorship. We also introduce a related concept, the parameter of the price of serial dictatorship, which we use to evaluate the efficiency of various optimization tasks described above by analyzing the relationship between this efficiency and the associated parameter. We discover that this efficiency is directly proportional to the largest minimum degree of nodes in these tasks. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. From an initial pool of 310,000 images, representing approximately 
70,000 distinct asteroids, we pinpointed 17 potential wide binary candidates, 
awaiting verification through high-resolution imaging. Among these candidates, 
the most plausible case involved the asteroid (45) Eugenia, previously known 
to comprise a close binary moon, for which we discovered evidence of a 
perturbing, longer-period orbital component. If confirmed, this would indicate 
that (45) Eugenia possesses a multi-body structure, further highlighting the 
complexity of its dynamics. If not, it would suggest that (45) Eugenia is 
entrenched in a temporary binary configuration, awaiting the release of 
small(er) components through eclipse events or other means. If this last 
scenario materializes, targeted astronomical observations during future 
eclipses could provide additional insights into (45) Eugenia's intricate 
dynamical makeup. Overall, detecting (45) Eugenia's suspected longer-period 
binary component, set within the realm of small to intermediate separations, 
presents a binary asteroid case study for the scientific community, with 
implications for the understanding of asteroid masses and the stability of 
binary asteroids. If verified, this discovery also highlights the capacity of

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established. The study also verifies the efficacy of these rules by applying them to solve two sample problems. Furthermore, it highlights the entropy of fractional processes as a key application of these new mathematical formulations. The results provided have been validated numerically using the Matlab software. The study's contributions are marked by the following key points. The first product rule type was initially introduced in 2013, but it has been found to be error-prone. The study offers four alternative product rule types, confirming the formulas proposed in 2013 but considering the order variable 'v' relative to the orders $\alpha$ and $\beta$. The study also extends the 2013 formulars to the quotient and chain rule types. The study's findings aim to enhance the understanding of complex fractional systems by providing a more accurate Leibniz Rule, which has been demonstrated through numerical examples of fractional differential equations. The study's main contributions are the new product, quotient, and chain rule formulas, while its secondary contributions include the Matlab software codes and the entropy metric for fractional processes. The study's outcomes have been published in various journals, including the Journal of Mathematical Analysis and its Applications, the Journal of Differential Equations, the IEEE Access journal, the Mathematical Methods in the Sciences and Engineering book series, and the Variable Order Differential Equations book series. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. By examining 147 protein structures with trefoil knots, our research demonstrates how the depth of a knot is influenced by the protein's folding dynamics and also highlights the challenges associated with experimenting on large knotted proteins in a laboratory setting. This study's insights into the folding dynamics of trefoil knots can be applied to biotechnological practices such as protein engineering. This involves identifying stable protein knots that are less challenging to fold and that maintain their three-dimensional structure even in the presence of heat or chemical stress. This goal is within reach due to the limited variety of knot types found in nature, which enables the thorough analysis of each type. This study's findings on the folding dynamics of trefoil knots can be utilized to develop predictive models that forecast the geometry of knotted protein folds based on their sequence data. This research's innovative approach to biologists, physicists, and mathematicians alike provides a unique perspective on knotted protein structures that are both biologically and mathematically significant. This knowledge can be further explored to understand the relationships between protein geometry, evolution, and folding dynamics. This study's results have been made publicly available through an interactive knotted protein explorer that enables users to browse through proteins with trefoil knots based on their sequence, structure, or folding dynamics. This explorer can be accessed at the following website: https://knotty.pro/. A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Finally, some intriguing connections between the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem have been presented. In closing, this work has been focused on the anomalous NG theorem with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures and has provided a comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon, which encompasses both the Heisenberg algebraic structure of the effective potential as well as the mode-mode interactions that generate mass within the NG sector. A study of this effective potential has also been found to be linked to both the geometry of symplectic structures and the number theory associated with transcendental numbers. A comprehensive examination has been conducted into which systems of particles are capable of exhibiting the anomalous NG theorem, which has been found to be a phenomenon that arises in closed systems with finite sizes. A key aspect of this investigation has been the introduction of a framework that can be used to study the effective potential in these systems, which has been found to be a natural consequence of the Weyl semimetal physics. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. We have made the code and an exhaustive set of experiments spanning our approach and accompanying benchmarks available for public access.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. It is also proposed that the increased domain size at lower growth temperatures could be beneficial for reducing disorder and improving the electrical properties of Heusler compounds. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The code has been made available openly for public use.  Future research will concentrate on developing a single network to generate class-conditionally conditioned synthetic data without the need for additional training beyond what is necessary for a single class.  The code has been made open for public use at the following link: https://github.com/zhayidong/Single-Positive-Conditional-Generation. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. It shows that the relationship between states and the associated C*-algebras is characterized by a symmetries-induced epistemology. We also establish that the weakly natural character of the abstract adjoint relationship enables the inclusion of non-trivial symmetries, which the associated physical system possesses, as an inherent component of the algebra's physical properties. This formulation can be viewed as a means of incorporating the concept of non-trivial intrinsic symmetries, which arise from the algebra's structure itself, into the definition of physical states. It highlights the significance of considering intrinsic symmetries when characterizing physical states and the associated observables in quantum mechanics. Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The code for FedHealth is readily available at https://github.com/liyouchuang/FedHealth.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies deemed "optimal" in the context of this problem. Our existing proof of the existence of an optimal policy relies on the ability to treat abrupt changes in costs as small jumps. An alternative existence proof is also possible using a different approach. Furthermore, we can determine the optimal policy by examining the underlying dynamics and the associated costs. This understanding enables us to classify the optimal policy into one of three categories: it can either be considered "good" if there are sufficient opportunities to switch to a state with lower cost; "bad" if there are not; or "indifferent" if the costs of switching are equivalent. This classification can be utilized to develop both a "reflective" barrier at which the optimal policy is willing to switch, as well as an "attractive" barrier that represents the minimum distance required to reach the next optimal state. Ultimately, this analysis lays the foundation for exploring more advanced control strategies, including those that consider both time horizons and multiple regimes. This work is an extension of recent studies on a related problem known as the M/M/1 queue, which involves prioritizing incoming calls. This extended version includes both an intuitive "gateway" example, as well as more formal "queue" and "switching control" examples. It is also relevant to the "optimal stopping' problems. It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
In both cases, we determine the minimum number of channels required to recover the
original transmitted sequence with a distance of 2r, or d = 5 and r = 4, not including the
channel itself.

of the Cayley graph in question, which we believe may be beneficial for understanding
the sequence reconstruction problem in this specific metric.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow-band PTA datasets. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package enables seamless access to searching for such eccentric signals within PTA datasets via the ENTERPRISE platform. The accuracy and efficiency of these methods are demonstrated through a mock data set derived from the NANOGravel scenario. The underlying ecosystem, consisting of the GWecc and ENTERPRISE tools, is designed to be a versatile platform with wide applicability, encompassing a wide range of gravitational wave models and PTA datasets. The PTA datasets and relevant ecns files are accessible at https://github.com/PTA-analysis/ptas. The nanogravel_ecn file used in the investigation is found at https://github.com/nanogravel/sim_data. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. In the latter scenario, we obtained an inelastic rigid pendulum model, which allows examination of magnetic bifurcation in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the formation of molecule-atom pair entanglements. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. Our approach also enables the sequence-independent retrieval of data from a segment by utilizing the PCR primer extensions alone. Our results demonstrate that our architecture yields a 10-fold decrease in the number of required sequencing reads for the retrieval of larger data objects, and facilitates the sequence-independent retrieval of data from a segment with a 2-fold decrease in the required number of sequencing reads. Our novel DNA-storage system's efficiency is showcased through the successful retrieval of multiple large data objects from a realistic, extensively validated dataset comprising 43 megabases of sequence data. Our research, along with the development of our novel DNA-storage system, involves a comprehensive analysis of the interplay between PCR addressing, sequencing read depth, and data object size, as well as the presentation of our own laboratory-derived primer-pair compatibility data. Our laboratory-tested methods and findings are further supported by publicly accessible data. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. This research provides a framework for a self-adaptive solver that can be integral to a flood management system, capable of incorporating updated riverbed data and adjusting the predictions accordingly. In this study, flow velocity predictions are shown to be more reliable than water level predictions, and future work is suggested to explore the integration of this approach with optimization algorithms for flood risk management. This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. The process involves transforming the problem into one involving oriented colored broken submersions through a minor expansion of the moduli space of curves, and this expansion is shown to be manageable through the mentioned precedents, ultimately leading to the solution of the standard Mumford Conjecture as a byproduct. The note also establishes that the class of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions is the most basic set of map functions, near to oriented submersions in 2 dimensions, that satisfy the b-principle, and in the process, provides an alternative proof of Harer's stability theorem. The research presented in this note was initially presented at the 2010 Kleinian groups conference held in Asheville, North Carolina. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. Overall, BDDC is found to consistently outperform AMG for the analyzed problems. Nonetheless, the efficiency of both solvers can be significantly improved through the use of more sophisticated BDDC neighborhood selection and higher-order Lagrange elements. Lastly, the project demonstrates a notable increase in efficiency when using 256 processors, stemming from a lack of efficient parallelization strategies certain solvers employ for small numbers of processors. The most efficient solution is identified as resulting from the BDDC algorithm using 256 processors, involving 1024 elements, and utilizing a direct solver for the local and coarse problem solutions. This most efficient solution requires approximately 0.29 seconds to solve per iteration. Additionally, the project involves a detailed examination of the scalability of both solvers, comparing the actual time required to solve the linear system against the ideal time scalpability is theoretically possible, and finding that both solvers exhibit subpar scalability. Consequently, the research recommends using both BDDC and AMG in conjunction with other solvers that exhibit better scalability, due to their superior solution characteristics, despite the solvers themselves exhibiting limited scalability. Nonetheless, the project demonstrates that both solvers can be efficiently employed to solve the type of complex problems it analyzed, despite the limited scalability, due to their ability to solve a significant portion of the system's degrees of freedom efficiently. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation. The theoretical analysis is validated through numerical simulations of a ring laser cavity. The developed approach can be a valuable tool for predicting the behavior of counterpropagating modes in cavities with waveguides and, by modifying the theory, it can also be used to analyze other resonator configurations. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. We've made the source code and environment publicly accessible to foster collaboration and innovation within the community.

Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online. Leveraging this approach and related research, we gather insights on process changes that may and may not be accurately captured by process models. These findings are relevant to various applications, including process improvement, quality control, and legal investigations. Our approach and associated tests can be found at this website: https://processchange.org/. Our research dataset is hosted at this repository: https://github.com/processchange/process-data. Our approach has implications for process monitoring systems, suggesting they should be based on robust, declarative processes that can survive temporary process deviations. Our results demonstrate that even slight process changes can significantly affect their likelihood, making process change analysis a non-trivial, probabilistic problem. Our approach provides a foundation for analyzing process changes from various sources, including employee feedback, management insights, and organizational analytics, allowing for the identification of most critical processes and areas requiring improvement, even in large, complex organizations. Our approach enables the calculation of the probability of process changes occurring, given observed processes, as well as the generation of most likely process change scenarios, as shown in the example analysis of a hospital patient flow process. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. The research highlighted the significance of considering the varied behaviors of galaxies based on their mass, especially in analyzing large datasets comprising thousands of galaxies. The study also emphasizes the value of the NUV$-r$ color as a reliable and easily obtainable indicator of star formation rate in massive galaxies, especially in the mass range greater than $10^{9}M_{\sun}$. The findings presented in the paper are applicable to various observational datasets featuring NUV and r-band magnitudes, including the one generated by the Next Generation Virial Black Hole Observation Project that will observe up to 50,000 galaxies with the Lucas Telescope. The knowledge gained from the research can be utilized in the analysis of future NUV and r-band magnitude combinations, combining multi-wavelength data from various observational projects. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory. However, W doesn't lift to the category of simplical rings in C due to a missing lift of the standard model structure to this category. Nevertheless, W does exhibit properties of a universal bundle functor for the category of simplicial rings in C. These results are achieved by introducing a more general concept of universal bundle functor, which is then applied to achieve the aforementioned findings. Additionally, it is proven that the category of simplicial rings in C lacks a universal bundle functor with coherent properties. Finally, it is demonstrated that the category of simplicial rings in any given C does possess a universal bundle functor, but this functor is not consistent with the conventional W when rings are viewed as groups. The findings presented in this research paper rely on the theoretical framework established in the works of Steedman, Berger, and Riehl and Verity. The key contributions of this study are an extension of the findings from the works of Steedman, Berger, and Riehl and Verity to a broader class of algebraic structures, and the discovery of a default universal bundle functor for the category of simplicial rings in any given C, along with an interpretation of this functor's behavior. The research discussed in this paper was initially presented at the 2018 TAC conference held in Leiden, Netherlands, and the TAC workshop held in Hanoi, Vietnam in 2018. The relevant proofs, examples, and additional discussion can be found in a supplementary document available at the following arXiv link: https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48550/arXiv.2206.00362. The related code can be accessed through the following GitHub link: https://github.com/EmmanuelKatz/simplicial_rings_universal_bundle. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/zwang84/SABRA. The dataset used in the research can be found at: https://github.com/zwang84/SABRA-Datasets. The feature extractor used in the experiments is Inception-5d, which can be found at: https://github.com/endernewton/resnet. The designed approach has the potential to be applied to other tasks with skewed proposal distributions. The datasets and code have been tested on 4 AMD EPYC 7702 64-core CPU and a single NVIDIA A100 40GB GPU. The research was conducted in accordance with the principles of fair testing as outlined in the benchmark: https://github.com/zwang84/SABRA-Benchmark.
