The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. The associated code is publicly available and has been optimized for GPU execution, showcasing a 1.5-3 times speedup over state-of-the-art deepfield-based methods on various large-scale sparse matrix applications. The algorithm's versatility allows it to be employed in a wide range of tasks, including neural network weight initialization, neural network optimization, and as a building block for other methods. The Nest Neumann method has the potential to serve as a foundational component for more advanced methods and has been designed with future GPU architectures in mind. The associated code release facilitates further optimization and enables the community to build upon this research. The Nest Neumann method has been tested on numerous large-scale matrix inversion applications, demonstrating its scalability and efficiency in the age of massive datasets. The code is implemented using PyTorch and Numpy, leveraging the benefits of both libraries to create a highly flexible and easily extensible framework. The Nest Neumann method has a number of advantages over other iterative methods, including a higher order of convergence, a smaller memory footprint, and the ability to handle complex matrices and sparse matrices with equal ease. The method's inception depth parameter also provides a level of adaptability that is unmatched by other methods, allowing it to be fine-tuned for optimal performance on a wide range of applications. The Nest Neumann method has the potential to be a game-changer in the field of linear system solving and matrix inversion

We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. Our results are relevant to real systems such as superlattice structures in optics or atomic gases, and can be experimentally realized in various topological Anderson insulating systems. Our theoretical framework is generally applicable to one-dimensional systems with on-site and nearest-neighbor disorders. We also discuss the extension of our results to two-dimensional systems with circulating disorders. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies. The research further explores the isomorphic connections between the curves defined by the sole non-trivial isogeny and those derived from different parameter representations. The investigation into isogeny curves reveals the existence of multiple curves within the same geometric class, each corresponding to a distinct order of the base curve, with orders determined by the discriminant of the curve's Jacobi invariant. The study emphasizes that the adoption of a reference point is essential to ensure that the computed periods yield a result of zero. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, agents that observe the context and make decisions are physically isolated from the learner. This learner executes the learning process but remains unaware of the context. Contexts are assumed to be generated randomly and a new approach is presented. This approach uses approximately five context dimensions' worth of information when the context distribution is unknown and uses zero bits when the distribution is known. This approach offers the first context-independent decentralized scheme. The proposed approach has the distinction of being the first context-independent decentralized scheme. Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Concerted efforts were made to rule out other possible causes of observed effects.  Events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow also display greater charged particle multiplicity, yet the relationship's strength is found to depend on centrality.  Ultimately, the findings are consistent with radial and elliptic flow's shared origins in initial state conditions, specifically properties of the collision system's intrinsic structure.  Analytical calculations utilizing the Glauber model and Monte-Carlo simulations utilizing the HYDRO+1 model support the proposed explanation.  Event Shape Engineering proves a valuable tool for uncovering the collision system's intrinsic properties and its effects on charged particle production.  Furthermore, the study emphasizes the importance of considering initial state conditions that predate quark gluon plasma formation and influencing radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Findings also highlight event Shape Engineering's capability to reveal charged hadron distribution modifications.  Charged hadron distributions modified by event Shape Engineering are found to agree with HYDRO+1 simulations utilizing the HYDRA solver for quark gluon plasma dynamics and semi-elastic hadron interactions with charged hadron production.  Charged hadron distribution modifications are found to be most evident in 30-40% most central collisions. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to binary power control generally being near optimal in everyday, non-long-term scenarios. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our simulation also revealed that artificially stretching collision time steps causes particles to be more likely to stick together after collisions, further confirming the importance of accurately modeling particle collisions. Our algorithm was found to be more stable and accurate even when artificially stretching collision time steps for evaluation purposes. Our simulation of sediment transport with artificial time stretching showed that particles can be up to 30d higher and the turbulence intensity can be up to 10 times greater than those observed with our algorithm, indicating that artificially stretching collision time steps can result in particles being too flexible and affecting the turbulence and distribution of particles. Our algorithm has been open to the public since 2022 and our code has been widely used in research simulations around the world. Our algorithm has been used in simulations of complex sediment transport with up to 50000 particles and has been tested on computers with up to 2048 processors. Our algorithm has been validated to be accurate when the ratio of collision time steps to the time steps used in flow simulations is between 2 and 64, however it can be used for ratios greater than this range with some adjustments. Our algorithm has been developed for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows and has been validated for algorithms that use multiple-time-step integration methods such as the semi-implicit and semi-lagrangian algorithms, however it can be used for other algorithms with some adjustments. Our algorithm has been tested to be accurate when the number of particles is between 100 and 50000, however it can be used for numbers greater than this range with some adjustments. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Ultimately, the robot was able to reach a height of 24.8 cm, only 0.2 cm shorter than the predicted height based on hopping simulations with the same muscle properties. This research confirms the efficacy of a feedforward-feedback force control system in regulating ground reaction forces during single-legged hopping on a granular surface. Moreover, it highlights the advantages of using a discrete element method simulator that incorporates a micro-scale model of the ground's composition to ensure the validity of simulations across different scale levels. Ultimately, this project contributes to the development of legged locomotion control systems that can adapt to varying terrain dynamics at multiple scale levels. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. The results show that our approach outperforms existing techniques in terms of accuracy, with the added benefit of being a session-free algorithm, allowing it to efficiently handle substantial amounts of data with minimal setup costs. Furthermore, our approach enables the creation of customizable hierarchical structures, facilitating the discovery of hidden patterns and relationships within complex information networks. We make our code and data available for further research and experimentation. The scalability and accuracy of HDTM make it a valuable solution for the automatic classification and categorization of large, interconnected information networks. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Thus, the one-band physics commonly applied to nickelates is shown to be
model-dependent, with varying outcomes based on screening, in turn affecting
the physics observed, from the local moment to the lattice-Kondo regime. 
Consequently, the one-band Hubbard model needs to be viewed with a critical
eye, being a specific, rather than a universal, representation of layered
nickelates. 
Furthermore, the interplay between lattice, electron-electron and electron-
phonon interactions is explored, finding that t$_{2g}$ orbital geometry hinders
both electron-electron and electron-phonon coupling, making it harder for
strong correlations to result in an insulating ground state. 
Lastly, the impact of reducing the number of electrons per unit cell from an
infinite layered configuration is examined, both with and without screening, 
finding that while it does cause an increase in electron-electron interaction 
strength, it also leads to a decrease in the extent of the Brillian zone, 
which in turn also contributes to a reduction in electron-electron interaction 
and may influence the one-band physics approximation even further.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.  Our research also reveals that the hybrid star equation of states is more resilient to the causality limit, which may facilitate the detection of quark matter through gravitational waves, especially in binary neutron star mergers with large mass ratio.  Finally, the density-dependent bag constant's parameterization is provided for future compact star simulations.  In the hybrid star case, the parameterization of the interface tension and bag constants is also offered for consideration in future pulsar radius measurements with high precision.  In the process, the characteristics of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index's density dependence are illustrated, which may influence the dynamics of neutron star mergers and their gravitational wave signals.  Notably, the density-dependent bag constant's parameterization can be utilized in models of neutron star and quark star mergers with compact star properties based on density.  Our work paves the way for a revised analysis of binary neutron star mergers with compact star properties based on density, which may be inferred from high-precision pulsar radius measurements combined with density-dependent bag constant parameterization.  This could, in turn, lead to a deeper understanding of the hadron-quark phase transition's properties, particularly the interface tension and bag constant's density-dependent behavior.  Ultimately, this knowledge can be utilized to re-examine the hadron-quark phase transition's oscillation patterns during binary neutron star mergers and their effect on gravitational wave signals as detected via LIGO and Vir

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. In addition, the reduced VSI in sinkingly settling disks aligns with observed decreases in shear velocity in these systems. Ultimately, the interplay between VSI, dust growth, and settling presents a complex, mutually-reinforcing cycle that most likely has a significant impact on the development and settlement of particles within protoplanetary disks. The key roles that VSI and dust play in its own stability, as well as that of surrounding environments, ensure that its effects will continue to be felt throughout a planet's formation. The research described in this report was part of a broader study examining the stability of protoplanetary disks. The modeling efforts described here served as a foundation for comparing stability with actual disk systems using a combination of observational and numerical data. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. Finally, simulations are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in real-world scenarios. This research has implications for the development of scalable and reliable Federated Learning systems. Code is available at https://github.com/Chenyue0821/WFRWDA. Although the current implementation is for Python-based NumPy and SciPy, it can be easily modified for other programming environments. Despite the challenges faced in this project, the results show that the proposed algorithm outperforms other random walk algorithms in terms of both convergence rate and accuracy. The code provided allows for easy replication of the experiment, enabling users to explore different parameter settings. The proposed WFRWD-A algorithm has been tested on various real-world datasets, demonstrating its superior performance in model convergence and accuracy when compared to other random walk algorithms. The code also includes an example of a small world random graph generation, which can be utilized as a baseline for comparing the proposed algorithm against other random walk methods. The generated code is valuable for the machine learning community working on Federated Learning systems. The code is part of the work contributed to the field of random walk learning algorithms and Federated Learning. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  A longer-term analysis estimating the cost of mental health treatment against the value of the decrease in future crime finds that for every additional dollar spent on treatment, there is approximately $1.40 in benefits as a result of the reduction in future crimes.  This study's results demonstrate the benefits of mental health treatment for offenders can extend far beyond their initial sentence and into the wider community.  It also highlights the potential cost-effectiveness of court-ordered mental health treatment as part of a sentence of probation.  Ultimately, it is essential to consider the longer-term consequences of providing mental health treatment to those within the criminal justice system and to explore the potential cost-benefit analysis of such treatment beyond the initial sentence period.  This research adds to the existing body of work examining the effectiveness of court-ordered mental health treatment within the justice system.  It contributes to the broader literature assessing the financial benefits of mental health interventions and provides valuable insights for policymakers, judges, and other key stakeholders within the justice system and public health sectors.  This study's results also have implications for the wider application of cost-benefit analysis in policy decision-making.  It is essential for policymakers and judges to consider the longer-term consequences of their decisions and the potential benefits of mental health treatment extending far beyond the initial sentence period.  This research demonstrates the potential of court-ordered mental health treatment to reduce future crime and the potential cost-effectiveness of such treatment.  It is, however, crucial to note that the magnitude of these benefits will depend on various factors including the type of treatment provided and the length of time offenders receive it for.  It is also vital to consider the potential limitations of the current study

It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing. We strongly advise against utilizing certain knowledge graph training and testing procedures that we have found to be flawed. We have made the code for this research available at https://github.com/zhoukaih1/deep-know-trace-analysis. Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. Furthermore, it is shown that if a Lie group $G$ has no compact components in its manifold form, then the operator $P$ is essentially surjective when defined as the set of second-order elliptic differential operators acting on vector fields on $G$. This is coupled with the observation that when the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ consists of solvable semisimple Lie algebras, the operator $P$ is also surjective on $\mathfrak{g}$. This leads to a proof that if the Lie group $G$ is solvable, then the group $C^\infty(G)$ forms a Helmholtz space. This implies that if the Lie group $G$ is solvable, the homogeneous Lie group $G$ possesses a distinguished Helmholtz decomposition, denoted as $\mathfrak{H}_0(G)$. This decomposition is characterized by the property that it is invariant under smooth left translations, making it a key result for further investigation. This is accompanied by an examination of the relationship between this concept and the spectrum of the Laplace operator on $G$. This is exemplified through the computation of $\mathfrak{H}_0(SO_2)$ and a related investigation of the eigenfunctions of the Laplace operator on $SO_2$ and its components. This reveals that they comprise orthogonal polynomials defined on compact intervals and their properties can be determined. This also leads to an examination of the relationship between Helmholtz decomposition and the theory of harmonic analysis on Lie groups. This includes an exploration of how this concept can be utilized to obtain results about the kernel of the Helmholtz operator and related information about its eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. This is a special case of a more general statement that can be applied to any group $C^\infty(G)$ with a Helmholtz decomposition $\mathfrak{H}(G)$. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. Simulations conducted on synthetic and real-world datasets, using up to 256 participants, demonstrate the effectiveness of this new FedBuff variant. The results show that this variant outperforms the original FedBuff algorithm in terms of convergence rate. The research and experimental findings highlight the FedBuff framework's potential to address practical challenges encountered in real-world federated learning applications. The FedBuff algorithm's advantages extend to the case where only server updates are available, making it a valuable contribution to the field of cross-device federated learning. The proposed variant has been successfully applied to classification problems involving up to 256 participants and diverse datasets, highlighting the durability of this framework. The code for this research is publicly accessible on GitHub, and the project has been deposited in the repository of the University of Colorado Denver. The current implementation utilizes PyTorch and TensorFlow as backend frameworks. The contribution of this study has been reviewed and approved by the University of Colorado Denver Institutional Review Board (IRB). The design of the research follows the guidelines set by the 2019 Federated Learning Workshop at IJCAI and the 2020 Federated Learning Workshop at AAMAS, emphasizing the importance of rigorous methodology in machine learning research. The project's repository includes detailed instructions for reproducing the results, adhering to the standards promoted by the Machine Learning Repository Excellence (MERITO) framework. The research and experimental findings presented in this study have been used in subsequent work conducted by the author, including the exploration of bias in cross-device federated learning and the development of methods to detect it. The FedBuff algorithm's versatility extends to task-oriented learning and multi-task learning, as demonstrated in the accompanying supplementary material. The project's repository also provides the underlying code and datasets used in the research, along with the results summarized in the accompanying tables and figures. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Notably, when we combined the transferred model with a fine-tuning model on a Czech dataset, we achieved a 19% decrease in WER when utilizing the Librispeech corpus and a 25% decrease when utilizing the Czech dataset NTKS04. We also successfully applied this technique to Slovak ASR. Notably, our approach was successful with a model trained on vast amounts of data from the internet, suggesting that the technique has vast potential for use with vast amounts of annotated data. We have made our code and trained models available for public use.

Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. Moreover, our model successfully addresses the pseudo data noise problem, eliminating the need for pseudo data correction, and enables efficient adaptation to new target domains at minimal cost, retaining 90% of its initial accuracy after 10 rounds of random domain jumps. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/zhuyonghu/metalgec.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we demonstrated that for any mechanism with any number of agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations, these equilibria are not guaranteed to be fair with respect to the underlying values, unless the mechanism involves a randomization with a finite number of possible outcomes, in which case the corresponding allocations are fair up to one good. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. Although these predictions generally hold true, some deviations from expected behaviors are observed in certain quark mass ranges. Furthermore, a comparison with predictions derived through the application of a sum rule technique in the framework of QCD is also presented. Conversions from lattice correlation functions to physical quantities are facilitated by fitting the output of chiral perturbation theory to the data. This approach allows for the determination of the pion's decay constant with enhanced precision as well as the extraction of low-energy QCD parameters in the chiral limit. These include the quark condensate, the slope of the slope of the quark condensate, and the ratio of quark currents to the pion's momentum within the quark sector. Our final calculations reveal a pion decay constant of 7.53 ± 0.17, a quark condensate of (341 ± 10) × 10^-3 and a value for the sigma parameter of (11.8 ± 0.4) × 10^-3. The research is conducted using the Improved Lattice Fermion code and involves the application of an improved stochastic estimator for the quark field correlations. This approach enables the extraction of quark field correlations with minimal bias for a wide range of quark masses. Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed relations in this context is hampered by
not properly accounting for variations in mass accretion rates, a problem
especially prevalent in earlier stages of star formation. Conversely, we found
large-scale fluctuations in mass accretion rates of one specific object, XX
Cha, and how these results could affect our current understanding of T Tauri
stars. Comparing our current analysis with previous measurements from the
X-Shooter, we observed a mass accretion variability of approximately 2 dex in
XX Cha over the 11-year period from 2010 to 2021, a value considered
particularly large among T Tauri stars. If this degree of variability holds
for other T Tauri stars on similar or different timeframes, then its effect
on the constraints of disk evolution models could be more pronounced than we
once anticipated, and it also highlights a potential shortcoming of earlier
research on mass accretion variability that relied solely on the study of
spectral lines, and thus, may have significantly underestimated variability
for certain objects. If the degree of variability we observed is indicative of
a longer-term phenomenon, then it could influence the mass accretion rates
we infer from observed relations, and as a result, a re-examination of the
relations themselves, as well as the physics that underlie them, is needed. 
Additionally, our analysis also reveals a 0.5 dex mass accretion variability
in the $d$-parameter, a measure of the ratio of high to low energy
recombination lines, over the 11-year period from 2010 to 2021, and we
interpret this as a sign of a somewhat shorter-lived 'burst' of mass accretion
activity on the order of a few years, and it could happen in certain T Tauri
stars more frequently than previously thought. 
Finally, if the variability we observed in XX Cha is typical of other T Tauri
stars, then it implies that even in the earlier stages of star formation and
planet formation, protoplanetary disks can experience 'fluctuations' in mass
accretion rates on various time scales, ranging from a few years to a few
decades, and it could also influence the formation and eventual migration of
planets within these disks.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Moreover, the theoretical foundation of our framework is supported by a discussion of the unfairness problem and suitable design constraints. We have publicly released our code and datasets to facilitate further research. We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Furthermore, we applied this technique to a real-world data set consisting of 10 head and neck patients, treated with conventional radiation therapy, and obtained promising, quantifiable results. Specifically, the 3D model yielded higher Dice similarity indices and smaller surface distances between registered treatment planning system images and actual megavoltage images, when compared to the 2D model. Nonetheless, the 2D model exhibited better results in capturing target structures' expansion due to patient movement between image acquisitions. Ultimately, our novel approach provides a viable alternative to traditional image registration techniques, particularly in situations with limited capture ranges, and the results encourage further testing with larger patient data sets. We have made the code and datasets available for public use.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Additionally, we highlight the limitations of using single-particle states for entanglement distribution and discuss various generating mechanisms for single-particle entanglement, including scattering processes and the action of external fields on entangled states of various particle compositions. Finally, we examine the suitability of these sources for realizing non-local effects via single-particle entanglement-generated steering. If the appropriate conditions are met, these sources can successfully implement truly non-local tasks while minimizing wasted time resulting from the random occurrence of particle entanglement. If the appropriate conditions are not met, we propose strategies for improving the efficiency of these sources. We also propose a novel approach for creating single-particle states with widespread, precise, and controllable non-local effects by utilizing a beam splitter to combine an external field with a pre-existing entangled two-particle state. V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate. V392 Persei's extensive evolution has given rise to several crucial observations: the massive transfer of matter through the system results in the formation of rays of both ejected and transferred matter that give off incredible amounts of energy; it also results in the formation of an extensive disk of matter that still exists even after nearly three years; and finally it has allowed the team to calculate the massive transfer of matter through the system, the large size of the companion that remains unchanged even after nearly three years, and the massive explosion that gave the system its incredible energy. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Simulation results demonstrate the system's capacity to adapt to changing environments and channel conditions, as well as the benefits of GMM-based design in cases where the base station can estimate the channel, revealing that this approach is robust and yields consistently better outcomes than traditional methods. Codebook reconfiguration is also leversaged to improve system performance. A proposed GMM training schedule involves the base station prioritizing a dynamic subset of GMM components based on the mobile terminal's reported quality indicator, ensuring the codebook remains adaptable to varying environment and channel conditions, thereby achieving a balance between exploring the signal distribution and avoiding excessive feedback. Through this approach, the system achieves a significant gain of approximately 12 dB at a 5 dB feedback load compared to the conventional method. Research demonstrates that the robustness of these currents can withstand various imperfections and tilting within certain nonequilibrium conditions. The need for true three-dimensionality also leads to a unique phenomenon where surface currents cannot exist on a lattice of any shape if the lattice is noncubic, and the robustness of boundary currents demands very small anisotropy. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our model predicts that the event GW190521 was likely produced by the merger of two pair-instability supernovae remnants rather than primordial black holes. Our study suggests that a significant portion of Population III binary remnants will form in the centres of galaxies and contribute to the formation of heavy elements through supernovae explosions. These remnants will also produce gamma-rays through the annihilation of weak interaction particles from the early universe, via the decay of neutrino-heavy element compounds, at a level that may be detectable by future telescopes. Our model predicts a gamma-ray signal of 10^-3 - 10^-2 photons cm^-2 s^-1 in the 10^8-10^9 eV energy range from the most massive of these remnants in the Milky Way's nuclear star cluster. If this prediction is confirmed, it would indicate that the formation of heavy elements and gamma-ray emissions in the centres of galaxies are more widespread than currently thought. Our study also shows that the most massive of these remnants will stall in the centres of galaxies with small half-light radii (r_\\half < 0.01 pc) and will be surrounded by a central massive star cluster with a total mass 10^3-10^5 M_\\odot. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. We demonstrate the importance of fast text-based games by showing that they significantly reduce testing time without compromising accuracy. Furthermore, we discovered that the current state-of-the-art text-based game agent, RRAM, falls short of its claimed performance due to an error in its original publication, necessitating a repeat evaluation to determine its genuine performance. Our optimized version is applicable to all current text-based game challenges and comes with an open-source code available on GitHub. Our research offers a meaningful improvement to the field of text-based game challenges, presenting a valuable resource for the community. Our goal is to encourage developers to adopt more efficient simulation technology to ensure that virtual agents continue to improve at a rapid pace. Our TextWorldExpress dataset is compatible with commonly used integrations such as PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Ray, making it accessible to a wide range of users immediately. Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. The designed FDHT-LSTM hardware also serves as a highly efficient LSTM-based video recognition platform that can be used in various real-world applications. The software of the FDHT-LSTM is publicly available on the following link: https://github.com/yangqiubo/FDHT-LSTM. The hardware blueprint can be accessed through the CSDN platform under the following link: https://blog.csdn.net/qq_43980625/article/details/12469501. The proposed FDHT-LSTM structure has been filed as a patent in the CN patent database (CN113448485A). Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. Based on the ring's properties and test elements, we find formulas to compute various coefficients, which are in turn used to establish the relationship between $F$-rationality and these coefficients, ultimately leading to the condition for $F$-rationality as depth $R \geq 2$ and a specific equality of these coefficients. The equality itself is achieved by examining the ring's tight Hilbert function and its connection to the parameter ideal, thereby establishing the connection between $F$-rationality and the tight Hilbert function. The paper's previous results on tight Hilbert functions, especially in a specific ring with a particular dimension, are obtained as consequences of its main results through ring transformation. The relationship between these tight Hilbert functions and their lower bounds are achieved by varying the parameter ideal, ultimately leading to the condition for $F$-rationality as a result of these variations. The paper also provides an analysis of its previous findings on tight Hilbert functions in the context of ring $R$ with a specific prime characteristic, considering its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, and exploring the relationship between these tight Hilbert functions and their lower bounds as depth $R \geq 2$ through the application of its characteristic to a regular local ring. The paper's contributions are characterized by its investigation of the tight Hilbert function of a specific ideal within a Noetherian local ring of a particular prime characteristic, making use of its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, and its examination of the condition for $F$-rationality as depth $R \geq 2$ and a specific equality of these coefficients. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. Nonetheless, the impact of these consequences on the entire system and particular agents is complex and depends on various market parameters and agent-specific behaviors. Hence, considering the design of redispatch markets is crucial for ensuring the reliability of the electricity network. R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. By examining the composition of the Galois group with automorphisms of the field k(t), we establish another connection – one that involves the permutation group Sn – when the polynomial F has a specific property called gl(2)-invariant. This leads to a computation of the number of irreducible polynomials with a particular property, offering a characterization of these polynomials as the ones whose Galois groups over finite fields are comprised of cyclic permutations of degrees 1 to d, where d is the polynomial's degree. This extensive analysis extends the scope of previous studies, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and its underlying field. The resulting theorems in this study can be applied to a variety of field-theoretic problems, especially those related to the distribution of irreducible polynomials within a given parameter range. The research also offers a framework for extending results in the literature, such as those related to the Bateman-Horn conjecture and the density of elliptic curves with a specific power level, to a wider range of parameters. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The reduction in the vortex's size during the equinoxes was attributed to the increased strength of these atmospheric waves as the planet's temperature differences between the equator and the poles decrease. The ultimate fate of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex was not observed as it was reaching the end of its typical lifespan, but models suggest it should have begun to break down and the chemicals it contained should have begun to spread to the mid-latitudes. This was not directly observed, but the decrease in the temperature difference between the poles and the mid-latitudes during the equinoxes could be an indication of this phenomenon. The study of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex has significantly enhanced the understanding of the processes that form the strong temperature differences seen in the Saturn system and has revealed the vital role that seasonal variations play in the formation of the polar vortices. The comprehensive analysis of the chemical composition of the vortex and the surrounding atmosphere has also facilitated a better understanding of the movement of chemicals in the Saturn system. The unique configuration of the Saturn system, with its extensive ring system, allows for the study of how particles move through the planet's gravitational field and influences the formation of the polar vortices. The interaction between the solar wind and the strong magnetic field of the Saturn system has a minimal impact on the polar atmosphere but influences the movement of chemicals in the system. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. It is essential to note that even though the optimal blow-up criterion in this case is identical to that in an infinite domain, the time it takes for a solution to reach the point of collapse may be significantly different compared to an infinite domain. This discrepancy is attributed to the impact of the focusing nonlinearity on solutions in the interior of the obstacle, as well as the effects of the obstacle's boundaries, which can significantly slow down the solution's approach to the point of collapse. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. Moreover, the algorithm's versatility can be extended to accommodate other x-ray sources and other spectroscopic techniques involving light-matter interaction. In addition to x-ray M\"ossbauer spectroscopy, this approach can be beneficial for the analysis of scattering off atomic and molecular targets. In such cases, the algorithm can facilitate a more precise extraction of information about potential energy levels and the temporal evolution of x-ray pulses. In x-ray M\"ossbauer spectroscopy, this approach can be used to investigate atomic and nuclear properties of various elements and compounds using a synchrotron radiation source. We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. Our approach's advantages are further highlighted by the notable improvement it exhibits over other existing methods when modeling blocking fractures, particularly in scenarios involving tightly packed fractures. This approach's potential is also shown to extend easily to multiple-phase flow applications. Our approach's preliminary form is made available through an open-source platform for public access. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. Evaluations conducted on this dataset reveal a high prediction accuracy for discourse indicators, despite variations in the underlying semantics, and provides a comprehensive analysis of predicted indicators in relation to existing classifications. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that using these predicted indicators as features enhances the performance of existing classification models in tasks like sentiment analysis and product aspect classification. Ultimately, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of discourse indicators in relation to semantic connections and offers a valuable resource, DiscSense, to the community. This dataset is distinct from existing datasets that annotate discourse relations but requires a separate characterization of discourse indicators. By exploring the relationship between discourse indicators and semantic connections, this work reveals that a universal classification system based on existing categorizations is unfeasible due to the diversity of relations and requires a more nuanced classification approach. Consequently, a new framework is proposed that is both universally applicable and categorized, and it is demonstrated that this characterization is relevant to various tasks and can be used to develop more effective feature extraction methods for English text. This research is an initial step towards a more comprehensive characterization of discourse indicators in languages other than English. The code and dataset are available at this link: https://github.com/zhuyong157/DiscSense.
