In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our approach is called the "Separate-Then-Share" dynamics model
enabler, and our code is available for public use. Our research contributes to
the understanding of dynamics models in multi-task settings and provides an
accessible framework for real-world applications. Our results highlight the
importance of careful model selection in order to leverage the benefits of
shared representations. Our approach can be viewed as a form of task-specific
domain adaptation, where the underlying domain is considered to be the same
for all tasks, and our dynamics model enables this adaptation. Our approach can
be used in any setting where the underlying dynamics of the environment remain
stable across different tasks or scenarios, and our code is designed to be
replicable and easily modifiable for the sake of scientific transparency. Our
research and code both contribute to the development of the field of multi-task
reinforcement learning. Our approach is called the "Separate-Then-Share" dynamics model enabler, and our code is publicly available. We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. We demonstrate how these theorems can be derived from a more basic result: given any sufficient formal system, there exists a specific sentence within the system's language that, when incorporated into the system, will yield a contradiction unless the system is incomplete. We explore the relationship between this result and the more well-known formulation of Godel's first incompleteness theorem, offering insights into the inherent limitations of formal systems in mathematics. We also touch on the potential extensions of this result to more complex, higher-order systems. Furthermore, we examine some notable discussions surrounding the status of the second Godel's Incompleteness Theorem in relation to the concept of undecidability. The original versions of these theorems were presented in the following papers: K. Godel, "Die formalen Theorien der osterreichischen Mathematischen Gesellschaft", Anzeiger der mathematischen Gesellschaft (1930); A. Tarski, "O pojasnieni pojecia prawdy w jezykach nauk dedukcyjnych" (1933); R. Carnap, "The Consistency of Formal Systems", Forum mathematicum 1 (1934); S. Rosser, "A Term whose Godel number is not its own", Anzeiger der mathematischen Gesellschaft (1936). We also consider some criticisms offered by the mathematician and philosopher, Willard Van Orman Quine. The synthesis of these theorems was initially outlined in the book "Godel's Way" by S. Kleene and J. B. Rosser in 1938, with later expansions presented in the works of Peter B. Andrews, particularly in his book "Arithmetical Logic" from 1963. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Additionally, our evaluations revealed that the generated samples accurately representative of the underlying data, surpassing the quality of those produced by Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, particularly in scenarios with limited training data. Our model was tested on various inverse problems and real-world images and we made the code publicly available. Our scheme leverages the capacity of the discriminator to provide valuable information about the posterior distribution, which facilitates the creation of realistic samples even when there is a significant gap between the prior and data. Our evaluations were conducted on scales up to 16384, which we believe represents the current practical limit for conditional Wasserstein GANs due to memory requirements. Our scheme generates samples that are meaningful and detailed, which we attributed to the incorporation of the Wasserstein metric, in contrast to the commonly employed Euclidean distance. Our model can be used for a range of applications, including optimizing cultural and social aspects, such as generating realistic avatars based on limited information, which we highlighted with an example. Our code is hosted on https://github.com/alexihc/wasserstein_saggan. Our evaluations showed that the quality of the generated samples improves significantly when the training set is increased, which we observed on scales up to 16384. Our scheme can be used in conjunction with other sampling methods to accelerate the generation process, which we demonstrated by substituting the noise injection method with our model, resulting in a 4 times speedup while maintaining the same Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metric. This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. Consequently, we emphasize the significance of examining fractional-order models with linear invariants due to the inherent properties of fractional dynamics. Ultimately, this discussion highlights the value of considering the stability of invariant sets when analyzing the behavior of dynamical systems. In doing so, we highlight the key differences between the dynamics of fractional and continuous systems. We also touch on the limited availability of numerical tools specifically designed to handle the stability of invariant sets in fractional-order systems. Nonetheless, we demonstrate how these sets can be utilized to grasp the asymptotic behavior of fractional-order systems by drawing upon a representative example. This example showcases a fractional-order Hermite-Hadamard inequality, whose stability is ensured through the examination of an invariant set in a fractional-order system. This discussion sets the stage for exploring the stability of the fractional-order Hermite-Hadamard inequality and related nonlinear integral equations. We conclude by highlighting the broader applicability of this approach to a wide range of nonlinear fractional-order systems. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This screen's distance, along with its observed scintillation pattern characteristics, suggests it is located very close to the Sun's orbital radius and is oriented nearly perpendicular to the Galactic plane. The investigation proposes it may be a key screen contributing to scintillation noise for a significant number of pulsars in the solar neighborhood. The screen's proximity to the Sun also implies it could significantly influence radio wave scintillation patterns affecting Earth-based telescopes, particularly those searching for the biosignature of extraterrestrial life. The discovery of this screen, with a possible physical relationship to the surrounding void, highlights the interstellar medium's complex structure and the need for further investigation into its effects on astronomical signals. The approach used in this analysis can be applied to long-term observations of other pulsars and Stokes I dynamic spectra of quasars and other compact sources to map scattering screens in the interstellar medium. The technique may also be used to investigate the distribution of screens at greater distances from the Sun, such as those influencing scintillation patterns observed in Earth-based radio frequency interference-free bands. The most notable finding from this analysis is the presence of a large screen with a distance of 5.46 parsecs, located very close to the Sun's orbital radius, oriented nearly perpendicular to the Galactic plane, and associated with a void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. The approach employed in this research can be applied to long-period observations of other pulsars and other compact sources to map scattering screens in the interstellar medium. The technique may also be used to investigate the distribution of screens at greater distances from the Sun, such as those influencing scintillation patterns

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Furthermore, QPNet is applied to generate waveforms for inputs outside the training frequency range, resulting in better performance compared to WN and other baselines. The proposed model's effectiveness is shown to be robust in various speech synthesis scenarios, extending beyond its primary application to other quasi-periodic signals and audio waveform generation tasks. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. The underlying Berman's THH cycle complex is then generalized to bicategories, with the resulting shadow framework exhibiting properties such as asymmetry, closure under composition, and adherence to Morita invariance. The connection between shadows and the norm functor for bicategories is also explored, along with the specific case study of the category of Banach algebras and Gelfand-Naimark duality. The theoretical shadow framework is thereby shown to be a natural extension of the classical algebraic shadows, preserving key characteristics and providing a broader, more generalized structure. The relationship between shadows and cyclic structures is explored through the representation of functors from THH as composites of natural transformations, with resulting shadows identifying the bicategorical crossed modules as the fundamental building blocks of a given bicategory. The study of Banach algebras via the theory of shadows ultimately leads to the incorporation of topological ideals within the framework, with the ideal construction itself being understood as a bicategorical crossed module, representing the underlying structure of a non-degenerate subfactor of a given C*-algebra. The connection between shadows and subfactors is further demonstrated through the consideration of certain K-theoretic invariants, with the resulting shadow crossed modules themselves being invariant under a modified notion of Morita equivalence, known as strong Morita equivalence. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our source code and datasets are available for public use at https://github.com/yangzw/SSLRV2.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Additionally, LGCN achieves comparable performance to the current best methods on more complex graphs at a lower distortion level, and it is shown that LGCN is robust across a range of hyperbolic parameters. This paper is an extended version of a previous paper that was published at the 2023 AAAI conference. This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Ultimately, this investigation leverages the Carleman estimate as a means to obtain a stability estimate. To this end, it employs a uniqueness result derived from a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, our exponential model can be applied to calculate
expected outcomes and utilities in economic decision-making, and it incorporates
the concept of impulsivity as a key factor. We demonstrate the applicability
and utility of this model by applying it to real-world economic decisions, and
it compares favorably to existing delay discounting models in terms of model
fitness. Additionally, our data reveal that delay discounting curves are
asymmetrically skewed. We propose that the Tsallis distribution can be a
quantitative indicator for assessing an individual's economic impulsivity. The
results of our study highlight the significance of considering the distribution
of delay discounts rather than simply adopting the commonly used hyperbolic
model, and they offer a novel approach for analyzing economic decision-making
impulsivity with a scientific basis. The proposed model is applicable to a broad
range of economic decision-making scenarios, and it can be utilized as a
framework for investigating the neural mechanisms underlying delay discounting.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  The harmonic gauge formulation also facilitates the investigation of the harmonic gauge-choose process in the context of a linearized massive gravity with a cosmologically preferred gauge, allowing for the computation of the mass term's coefficient as it relates to the harmonic gauge choice.  The analysis is performed within the context of a linearized massive gravity with a cosmologically preferred gauge, previously proposed by Clunie and Leineker, where the choice of gauge is connected to the harmonic gauge and results in the emergence of the five linearly polarized degrees of freedom we seek.  The investigation entails a mathematical and physical analysis of the harmonic gauge-choose process in a linearized massive gravity with a cosmologically preferred gauge, exploring the interplay between the harmonic gauge and the mass term's coefficient.  The implications of this investigation are far-reaching, offering insights into the interplay between the harmonic gauge and the mass term's coefficient in a linearized massive gravity with a cosmologically preferred gauge. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. Examples from the 4d and 5d transition metal oxides with spinel, perovskite, and BaRuO$_3$-related structures demonstrate the necessity of considering $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing in assessing their physical behavior. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our research, a pioneering effort in medical imaging using GANs, presents a promising approach to addressing future healthcare challenges. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application is particularly suited for
experts in science who require an intuitive and graphical approach to
statistical analysis. ViDaExpert is available for Windows platforms. The article
also briefly addresses the underlying mathematical principles underlying the
implemented algorithms. The source code of ViDaExpert is provided as supplemental material.
